strengths: The core idea—optimizing a region-specific embedding at inference time by matching its explanation map to a supplied mask—is interesting and avoids backbone fine-tuning or input-image modification.
The learned representation is evaluated across several applications and datasets, including region classification, referring-expression retrieval, captioning, and qualitative image generation.
The reported classification and retrieval improvements over reproduced CLIP, masked-crop, FGVP, RIS, and AlphaCLIP baselines are substantial.
The paper includes useful analyses of mask degradation, explanation-method choice, backbone scaling, and the runtime effect of gradient decomposition.
weaknesses: The central gradient-decomposition derivation appears incorrect as written. Equation 2 defines the score using cosine similarity, but Equation 6 replaces its derivative with a Jacobian-vector product involving LET while omitting cosine normalization and projection terms. This undermines the claimed equivalence and makes the actual implementation unclear.

The proposed decomposition seemingly requires the large Jacobian d(z-bar)/dA with shape h×n×n×d, yet its memory and computation are not analyzed. Runtime results lack hardware, memory, batch-size, and end-to-end comparisons, and decomposition is slower for five masks.

The referring-expression protocol is internally inconsistent: the text describes selecting a mask for an expression, whereas Table 1 describes retrieving an expression from a query mask. Ground-truth masks create an oracle-proposal setting that is not directly comparable to several cited methods, weakening the SOTA claim.

The captioning evaluation uses CLIP similarity to match generated captions to referring expressions, closely coupling evaluation to the CLIP-derived representation being optimized. There are no standard caption-quality metrics, human evaluation, or tests with additional captioners.

The broad claim of compatibility with any pretrained model is unsupported. Experiments use only CLIP-family ViTs, and the explanation-method ablation shows extreme dependence on LeGrad: PascalVOC Acc@1 falls from 85.4 with LeGrad to 47.6 or lower with alternatives.

Essential ablations and reproducibility details are missing, including the effect of the regularization weight, performance versus optimization iterations, learning rate and other optimizer settings, prompt templates, exact splits and OpenImages subset construction, statistical uncertainty, and evidence that the decomposed implementation matches the original optimization.

Presentation errors further reduce confidence: the project-page link is blank, Table 2 reports an implausible 8.9 Acc@10 for ViT-B/32, and the explanation ablation is described as MSCOCO in the text but PascalVOC in the table caption. Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but the central mathematical inconsistency and evaluation ambiguities are too substantial for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful test-time approach for extracting mask-conditioned regional embeddings from a frozen vision-language model.
The empirical study covers several applications and datasets, including referring-expression retrieval, class retrieval, localized captioning, and qualitative diffusion experiments.
The reported class- and expression-retrieval improvements are often substantial, and the comparisons include several reproduced baselines using a common CLIP backbone.
The paper includes useful analyses of mask degradation, backbone scaling, explanation-method choice, and runtime as the number of masks increases.
weaknesses: The central gradient-decomposition derivation appears technically incorrect or seriously incomplete. Equation 2 defines the score using cosine similarity, but Equation 6 differentiates it as though it were an unnormalized dot product, omitting derivatives of both norms. No approximation or normalization assumption is stated. This undermines a claimed methodological contribution and leaves unclear what was actually implemented.

The decomposition is insufficiently specified and raises major feasibility questions. The stated cached Jacobian has shape h×n×n×d, which can be prohibitively large at the reported 448×448 resolution, especially for ViT-H/14. Memory consumption, implementation details, numerical equivalence, and hardware are not reported.

The evaluation does not establish fully fair comparisons. The appendix reveals that MaskInversion increases CLIP inference resolution from 224×224 to 448×448, but it is unclear whether reproduced baselines receive the same resolution. The paper also combines results from materially different referring-expression protocols, so several apparent state-of-the-art comparisons are not directly meaningful.

The referring-expression task is framed unusually: ground-truth masks are supplied and expressions are retrieved among candidates, whereas much prior work starts from an expression and localizes it using proposals. This greatly changes the problem and limits the significance of comparisons to reported prior results.

The localized-captioning evaluation is weak. Its sole metric ranks a generated caption against referring expressions using CLIP similarity; this does not directly measure caption correctness, fluency, factuality, or grounding and may favor embeddings aligned with CLIP. There is no human evaluation, standard caption metric, or analysis of failure cases.

The diffusion evidence is entirely qualitative, contains only a few favorable examples, and lacks comparisons against competing localization methods. It therefore does not substantiate claims of broad downstream applicability.

The claimed generality is overstated. Experiments are confined to CLIP-style ViTs, and performance depends dramatically on LeGrad: accuracy reportedly falls from 85.4 with LeGrad to 47.6 or lower with alternative explanation methods. This suggests a tightly coupled construction rather than compatibility with arbitrary pretrained models and differentiable explainers.

Important ablations are missing, including the regularization weight and its accuracy/context trade-off, initialization choices, optimization hyperparameters and convergence, inference resolution, and comparison against simpler feature-pooling or optimization baselines. No variance or statistical uncertainty is reported.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the project-page field is blank, while learning rate, weight decay, class-prompt templates, dataset splits and sample counts, OpenImages subset construction, preprocessing, hardware, runtime units/protocol, and memory costs are omitted. There are also reporting inconsistencies, such as Table 6 being described as PascalVOC in its caption but MSCOCO in the text.

strengths: MaskInversion offers a clear and useful contribution: it derives a mask-conditioned regional embedding from a frozen vision-language model through test-time optimization, without retraining the backbone or modifying image pixels.

The learned embedding is genuinely versatile. The paper demonstrates the same representation in region classification, referring-expression retrieval, localized captioning, and diffusion-based visualization, supporting the claimed drop-in applicability.

The empirical results are strong across PhraseCut, RefCOCO/+, PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, and OpenImagesV7. Same-backbone comparisons are generally favorable, with especially large gains on several class-retrieval benchmarks.

The paper includes useful studies of mask degradation, backbone scaling, attribution-method choice, optimization progress, and the runtime benefit of gradient decomposition when many masks are processed.
The method is intuitive, reasonably well motivated, and its dependence on mask and explainability quality is acknowledged.
weaknesses: The gradient-decomposition derivation is not mathematically consistent with the stated cosine-similarity score. Equation 6 treats the score as linear in the localized embedding and omits cosine-normalization terms; the paper should either provide the correct derivation or clarify that normalized features reduce the score to a dot product.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the learning rate and other optimization details, prompt templates, exact dataset subsets and splits, hardware, memory usage, and several preprocessing choices are missing. The displayed project-page link is also empty.

Some state-of-the-art claims overstate the evidence. Comparisons marked with a dagger use incompatible protocols and backbones, while MaskInversion with ViT-B/16 does not uniformly beat Masked Crop on RefCOCO+. The strongest results also use a substantially larger ViT-H/14 backbone.

Localized captioning is evaluated through a CLIP-based retrieval proxy rather than established caption-quality metrics or human judgments. This can reward semantic overlap without establishing caption correctness or fluency. The diffusion evaluation is qualitative and too small to support strong general conclusions.

The efficiency analysis reports only latency for one backbone and unspecified hardware. It does not examine memory consumption, per-mask optimization cost in realistic workloads, or the potentially large Jacobian implied by the decomposition. The method is slower than the undecomposed version for five masks.

Several presentation inconsistencies need correction, including an apparently erroneous 8.9 Acc@10 entry for ViT-B/32 on PascalVOC and a mismatch between the dataset named in the explanation-method ablation text and its table caption.

strengths: MaskInversion is a novel and intuitive test-time approach: it optimizes a single region embedding so that its attribution map matches a supplied mask, while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen.

The empirical results are consistently strong across several classification and referring-expression datasets. In particular, the same-backbone comparisons with MaskCLIP, CLIP Surgery, and SCLIP show substantial improvements across multiple CLIP architectures.

The paper explores a broad range of applications and includes useful analyses of mask perturbations, optimization convergence, the local-global regularization weight, backbone scaling, and alternative explainability methods.
The proposed gradient decomposition addresses an important practical cost of per-mask optimization, and the paper reports increasing benefits when many masks are processed for an image.
weaknesses: The reproducibility details are insufficient. The paper omits essential information such as the optimization learning rate and weight decay, explainability-map normalization, prompt templates, dataset splits and sample counts, baseline hyperparameters, hardware and timing methodology, and whether hyperparameters were selected on held-out validation data. No code or release commitment is stated.

The gradient-decomposition analysis is incomplete. The proof drops the cosine-normalization terms and only argues that the token is independent of the activations; it does not derive the actual normalized expression. More importantly, precomputing the stated Jacobian can have very large memory and computational complexity, but neither complexity nor peak memory is reported. The claim of linear resolution scaling is based on five timing points without uncertainty, hardware details, or comparison to the undecomposed implementation.

Some evidence does not support the breadth of the claims. All quantitative backbone experiments use CLIP, and performance depends dramatically on the attribution method: LeGrad obtains 85.4% on PascalVOC while GradCAM and CheferCAM obtain 34.6% and 12.6%. Thus, the claim that the method applies broadly to any pretrained model or differentiable explanation method is not demonstrated.

The referring-expression protocol selects among ground-truth masks and differs substantially from standard referring-expression comprehension. Although this is partly disclosed, the presentation of prior published numbers with incompatible proposal-based protocols alongside the new results can be misleading. The paper also lacks evaluation against learned region-level vision-language encoders under a carefully matched protocol.

The localized-captioning metric only asks whether a CLIP text encoder ranks the generated caption closest to the target expression among expressions from the same image. It does not directly measure caption correctness, coverage, fluency, or hallucination, and may favor embeddings aligned with CLIP. The diffusion application is purely qualitative, so neither application provides strong evidence for the claimed general downstream utility.

Important component ablations are missing, including comparisons of initialization strategies, Dice loss against simpler mask-alignment objectives, and regularization effects across all tasks. There are also reporting inconsistencies: the text describes the attribution-method experiment as being on MSCOCO, whereas Table 8 labels it PascalVOC. Overall, the promising core idea and strong retrieval results are slightly outweighed by unresolved technical, protocol, and reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The central idea—optimizing a region-specific embedding by matching its attribution map to a supplied mask—is intuitive, potentially useful, and meaningfully different from modifying pixels or fine-tuning the backbone.

The paper evaluates region embeddings across several datasets and CLIP backbone sizes, and includes matched-backbone comparisons with strong baselines such as AlphaCLIP, MaskCLIP, CLIP Surgery, SCLIP, RIS, and visual-prompting methods.
The reported class-retrieval and referring-expression results are often substantially better than the reproduced baselines, rather than merely incremental.
The analyses of mask perturbations, optimization iterations, regularization strength, attribution methods, and runtime expose several relevant aspects of the method.
weaknesses: The gradient-decomposition derivation is not technically sound as presented. The method defines the attribution score using cosine similarity, but the derivation replaces it with a dot product and declares the decomposition mathematically exact. Cosine normalization introduces additional terms. The paper neither derives these terms nor demonstrates that the implemented approximation is equivalent.

The computational account is incomplete and questionable. The stated Jacobian has shape h×n×n×d and could be extremely large, especially for the reported 448×448 inputs and larger ViTs, yet memory consumption, implementation details, and comparison with ordinary inference are absent. The claimed linear scaling with token count is also insufficiently reconciled with the quadratic attention/Jacobian dimensions.

Reproducibility is weak: the manuscript does not provide code or enough information about dataset splits, sample counts, OpenImages subset construction, class prompts, preprocessing, batching, hardware, random seeds, or uncertainty. Alpha and the number of optimization steps appear to be selected using downstream performance on the reported datasets without a clearly separate validation protocol.

Some central claims are broader than the evidence. The experiments cover CLIP ViTs, and the attribution-method ablation shows performance collapsing from 85.4 with LeGrad to 12.6–47.6 with alternatives. This does not support compatibility with arbitrary pretrained models or differentiable explanation methods.

The referring-expression protocol is ambiguously described: different passages alternately frame it as retrieving a mask from an expression and retrieving an expression from a mask. Published numbers obtained with region proposals are included despite being explicitly incomparable, while candidate construction and metric aggregation are not specified sufficiently for independent reproduction.

The localized-captioning metric is a nonstandard CLIP text-similarity retrieval proxy. It does not directly evaluate caption correctness, completeness, or fluency, uses only one captioner, and lacks human evaluation. The diffusion evidence is entirely qualitative and susceptible to example selection, so these application claims are not convincingly established.

There is no control isolating whether gains arise from meaningful image semantics versus mask geometry or the flexibility of fitting a high-dimensional attribution basis—for example, shuffled image-mask pairs, random/frozen features, shape-only inputs, or similarly optimized pooling baselines.

The efficiency advantage is narrow: decomposition is slower at five masks and only becomes beneficial when processing many masks. End-to-end latency and memory are not compared fairly with the single-pass baselines, limiting the practical significance of the claimed computational improvement.

The paper does not discuss inherited CLIP biases, misuse risks for generated content, or other ethical limitations. Overall, the strong reported accuracies are promising, but the mathematical inconsistency and insufficiently specified evaluation prevent confidence in the central claims.

strengths: MaskInversion is a clear and interesting test-time approach: it learns a mask-localized embedding while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen, avoiding additional mask-text training data.

The empirical results are compelling. Across PhraseCut, RefCOCO/+, PascalVOC, PascalContext, COCO, and OpenImagesV7, the method generally outperforms strong reproduced baselines, including AlphaCLIP, FGVP, RIS, MaskCLIP, CLIP Surgery, and SCLIP.

Evaluation across several CLIP architectures shows consistent scaling, with especially substantial improvements for larger backbones. The use of common evaluation protocols for the reproduced methods makes these comparisons more informative than comparisons to originally reported, incompatible settings.

The paper includes useful analyses of mask degradation, optimization convergence, the local-context regularization tradeoff, explainability choices, resolution scaling, and gradient-decomposition runtime. Localized captioning and diffusion examples also illustrate the representation's versatility.
The method is conceptually simple and practically appealing: its output is a single embedding that can be inserted into downstream components expecting a CLIP image representation.
weaknesses: The gradient-decomposition derivation is not exact as written for the cosine similarity defined in Eq. 1. Equations 5–11 replace cosine similarity by a dot product and omit normalization derivatives; the appendix asserts that this does not affect the derivation, but it does affect the stated formula. An exact derivation for the implemented score, or clarification that normalized representations and their Jacobians are used, is needed.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as the AdamW learning rate and weight decay, prompt templates, dataset splits and sample counts, construction of the 350-class OpenImages subset, mask preprocessing, baseline hyperparameters, and runtime hardware are missing or underspecified. No code or release commitment is stated.

The broad claim that the approach can use any differentiable explanation method is not well supported: performance varies drastically from 12.6 with CheferCAM and 34.6 with GradCAM to 85.4 with LeGrad. This suggests substantial dependence on a specialized attribution method.

The captioning evaluation uses CLIP similarity to referring expressions rather than standard caption-quality metrics or human evaluation. Because CLIP is also central to the method, this proxy may favor outputs aligned with the same representation space. The diffusion evidence is qualitative only, so the strongest support is for retrieval/classification rather than all claimed applications.

Some experimental choices appear tuned without a clearly identified validation protocol, particularly alpha=5 for RefCOCO/+. There are also inconsistencies such as the Table 8 discussion naming MSCOCO while the caption and reported value indicate PascalVOC, and ambiguity over whether referring-expression retrieval maps masks to expressions or expressions to masks.

The method performs per-mask test-time optimization and only becomes faster than the undecomposed implementation when processing more than roughly five masks. Comparisons of end-to-end latency, memory, and accuracy-efficiency against direct pooling or masking baselines would better establish practical utility.
